newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt closes sharply weaker, hit by U.S. selling.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt closes sharply weaker, hit by U.S. selling.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 91.93 (PREV 92.05) 90-DAYS 7.93 (PREV 7.85)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.45 PCT (PREV 7.50) US 5-YR 6.72 (PREV 6.71)
* NZ debt underperforms on spreads after U.S. selling
* Bearish sentiment takes grip on money market too
* U.S. data seen setting scene for short term
New Zealand bond yields were hit hard on Thursday by selling right across the curve by a local bank, on behalf of U.S. interests.
The 11/06 bond ended 10 basis points higher at 8.15 percent, and one dealer suggested that if it broke through major support at 8.20 percent a move to around 8.50 percent was on the cards.
He said the U.S. selling was probably a result of position adjustment in the new financial year.
The mid bonds finished 13 basis points weaker at 8.09 percent.
Dealers said there seemed to be a reasonable number of bonds given out, as the market had failed to bounce back.

The bearish sentiment took its toll on the money market as well, where 90-day bank bills finished eight basis points higher at 7.93 percent despite the fact that the currency's Trade-Weighted Index ended on its open of 68.19.
The June futures contract closed down 11 points at 91.94 (8.06 percent) on heavy volume of 3,603 contracts.

A NZ$50 million government tender of February 2016 inflation indexed bonds was not well-supported, attracting only $84 million in bids. The bonds yielded 5.38 percent against the 4.84 percent yield from the last tender on February 13.

ANZ Bank senior manager of domestic markets Jim Reardon said that to some extent, New Zealand debt markets could be anticipating weakness in U.S. Treasuries on the back of weekly job claims data due tonight (NZ time) and U.S. non-farm payrolls data on Friday.
"The important level for me at the moment is that the U.S. 30-years shouldn't break 7.20 percent," he said.
"If we get a close in the U.S. 30s above 7.20, I would say that's going to be bad for New Zealand and Australia.

"Given how far we've come on the selling in New Zealand and given where the spread is now, I would suggest that if the U.S. market rallies now, we will rally quite strongly with it, because I would have thought we were starting to get a little bit short," Reardon said.
The U.S. 30-year Treasury yield is currently 7.08 percent.
